title: Gilliam County Historical Museum
contentHtml:
The Gilliam County Historical Museum is a complex of century-old buildings on Highway 19 next to Burns Park in Condon, including an 1884 homestead, a 1905 railroad depot, an authentic one-room schoolhouse, a church, agricultural exhibits and a building that was once a brothel and later a barbershop.

Its collections remember the pioneers whose wagons crossed the county on the Oregon Trail, and past residents including Tonight Show musician Doc Severinsen and Nobel Prize winners Linus Pauling and William Murphy.

title: John Day Crossing Historic Site
imageAlt: Sunset at the John Day Crossing Historic Site

banner.alt: Sunset at the John Day Crossing Historic Site

gallery.alt: The Oregon Trail's hillside descent to the crossing

contentHtml:
John Day Crossing Historic Site marks where two branches of the Oregon Trail met at the lower John Day River. White markers on the hillside show where the wagon routes descended, and an interpretive site about a quarter mile up the road overlooks the crossing. Emigrants who came down one branch reportedly joked that the other 'could not be worse than the one they descended.'

A small primitive campsite sits in a cottonwood grove, with picnic tables and a vault toilet, and a primitive boat launch is the last public takeout on the John Day Wild and Scenic River above Tumwater Falls.

title: Thirtymile Recreation Area
contentHtml:
The Thirtymile Recreation Area is about 20,000 acres of BLM land on the east side of the John Day River, taking in parts of Armstrong Canyon, Thirtymile Creek and the river. It was acquired in 2018-19.

A primitive boat ramp just upriver from the mouth of Thirtymile Creek has trailer parking and a boating kiosk, and dispersed camping is allowed in the cleared field near the launch until a campground is built. Foot, bike and horse access continues up the old roads and Thirtymile Creek.

note: No fee. Armstrong Rd is unimproved dirt and rock, open to vehicles April 1 to December 14; high clearance recommended, and it can be impassable when wet. No toilet, drinking water, trash or cell service; pack out all waste. No campfires June 1 to October 15. A launch permit from Recreation.gov is required year-round to boat between Service Creek and Tumwater Falls.
address: End of Armstrong Rd at the John Day River, about 10 miles southwest of Condon, OR

title: Willow Creek Wildlife Area
contentHtml:
Willow Creek Wildlife Area protects 646 acres at the mouth of Willow Creek on the Columbia River, one of four ODFW wildlife areas in the Columbia Basin. Its wetland, sagebrush-steppe and grassland habitat draws white pelicans, black-crowned night herons, great egrets, waterfowl, shorebirds, songbirds and California quail.

Visitors can fish, hunt, launch a boat and explore on foot from the parking lot.

note: An ODFW Wildlife Area Parking Permit is required ($10/day, $30/year). No camping or open fires. From exit 151, head south on Threemile Canyon Rd about half a mile and turn right at the wildlife area sign; traffic passes a private-land security checkpoint, so say you are going to the wildlife area and follow the signed route.
address: I-84 exit 151, Threemile Canyon Rd, between Arlington and Boardman, OR

title: Northwest Discovery Water Trail
imageAlt: Earl Snell Memorial Park on the Columbia in Arlington (area photo)

banner.alt: Earl Snell Memorial Park on the Columbia in Arlington (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Northwest Discovery Water Trail is a 367-mile boating route from Canoe Camp on the Clearwater River in Idaho, down the Snake River and the Columbia to Bonneville Dam in the Columbia River Gorge. More than 150 sites along the way are for launching, picnicking or camping, for motorboats, canoes, sailboats and kayaks.

In Oregon it follows the Columbia's south shore through Umatilla, Morrow, Gilliam, Sherman, Wasco, Hood River and Multnomah counties. Much of it is flatwater behind eight dams, with locks to pass through or portage around.

note: Always wear a life jacket. Check forecasts for high winds and storms, yield to commercial barges and their wakes, and watch for submerged stumps and debris. Plan each dam lock-through or portage before you go.
address: Columbia River south shore, including Arlington, OR

title: Lost Valley of Condon
imageAlt: On the Lost Valley of Condon route

banner.alt: On the Lost Valley of Condon route

contentHtml:
Lost Valley of Condon is a 44-mile loop of about 60% gravel and dirt with about 3,500 feet of climbing, past farm fields, basalt canyons and cottonwoods. It heads south on a paved downhill past tall basalt cliffs, then climbs onto the plateaus to its high point near the southern tip.

Late spring brings green hills and late fall brings orange, yellow and taupe colors. The loop can be ridden in either direction.

title: John Day River
contentHtml:
The John Day River is the longest undammed river in Oregon. Its 147.5-mile recreational section from Service Creek to Tumwater Falls was designated a Wild and Scenic River on October 28, 1988, running through colorful canyons, broad valleys and high desert, with basalt cliffs over 1,000 feet high.

It holds one of the region's few remaining wild runs of summer steelhead and spring Chinook, plus prime smallmouth bass water, and the Oregon Trail crossed it at McDonald Ford. Boating is mostly calm with a few rapids; the corridor also offers camping, swimming and wildlife watching, including bald and golden eagles, bighorn sheep and elk.

title: John Day River Farm Trail
contentHtml:
The John Day River Farm Trail is a food-focused drive along the John Day River, where small valleys hold lush grass, alfalfa, gardens and fruit orchards. More than 30 stops run from John Day through Kimberly, Spray, Fossil and Condon to Arlington: farms and orchards, farmers markets, breweries, ranch stays, outfitters and museums.

In Gilliam County, stops include the Gilliam County Museum, the Condon Community Summer Concert and Artisan Market, Cottonwood Canyon State Park and the Arlington Farmers Market.

title: Lonerock
contentHtml:
Lonerock, about 20 miles east of Condon, is one of the smallest incorporated cities in Oregon, with 25 residents at the 2020 census. It is named for a 35-foot rock that still stands beside the old Methodist church.

Platted in 1882 as Lone Rock, a service center for nearby ranches, it became one word because the post office preferred one-word names. It once had a jail, a school and a rodeo on Main Street, peaked at 82 residents in 1930 and never unincorporated. The white Methodist church, built in 1898, still stands and occasionally holds services.

title: Condon Wind Farm Viewpoint
imageAlt: Wind turbines above yellow fields near Arlington (area photo)

banner.alt: Wind turbines above yellow fields near Arlington (area photo)

contentHtml:
The Condon Wind Farm Viewpoint is a signed pullout on OR 206 just northwest of Condon, facing east to watch the turbines turn on the plateau skyline. Shepherds Flat, among the largest wind farms in the world, spreads across the Morrow County line northeast of town, with turbines rising more than 250 feet above the rangeland.

It is the nearer of two wind-farm viewpoints on the Condon highway.

title: Wind Farm Viewpoint
imageAlt: Wind turbines above yellow fields near Arlington (area photo)

banner.alt: Wind turbines above yellow fields near Arlington (area photo)

contentHtml:
Wind Farm Viewpoint is the farther of two signed wind-farm viewpoints on OR 206 west of Condon. It carries a peak-identification board naming the Cascade peaks on the western skyline, with the plateau's turbines turning in the foreground.

Its companion, the Condon Wind Farm Viewpoint, is closer to town on the same highway.
